note: A deed of gift came before Rav Yosef signed by two witnesses who were brothers-in-law. He wanted to accept it, since Shmuel had ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yosei, whom he understood to allow brothers-in-law. Abaye asked how he knew Shmuel meant that version of Rabbi Yosei's view, and the two argued over what Shmuel meant when he said he and his brother Pineḥas could not testify together. Rav Yosef then told the holder to take possession through the witnesses who saw the deed handed over. When Abaye objected that even then a deed with invalid signatures is invalid, Rav Yosef told the man: go, the rabbis will not let me give it to you.
why: The discussion is about which in-laws may not serve as witnesses, and has just cited Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Yosef tries to apply it, and Abaye shows that it is unclear which version of Rabbi Yosei's view Shmuel meant.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who first wanted to accept the deed and finally sent its holder away.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who challenged each of Rav Yosef's reasons.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose ruling on Rabbi Yosei is in question.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Early Sage whose view on brothers-in-law as witnesses is debated.

terms.meaning: A document recording that property was given as a gift, signed by two witnesses.
In Rabbi Elazar's view a document takes effect through the witnesses who see it handed over, not those who sign it.
Here, men married to two sisters.

note: The descendants of Ishmael and of Keturah took the Jewish people to judgment before Alexander of Macedon, claiming a share of the land of Canaan, since the Torah calls both Ishmael and Isaac sons of Abraham. Geviha ben Pesisa asked the Sages' leave to argue: if he lost, they could say only an ordinary man was beaten; if he won, that the Torah of Moses had won. He asked his opponents for their proof; they said: the Torah. He answered from the Torah: Abraham gave all he had to Isaac, gave gifts to his concubines' sons and sent them away. A son sent away by a father who divided his property in his lifetime has no claim on the other. The outcome is not told here.
why: This is one of a series of cases in which Geviha ben Pesisa argued for the Jews before Alexander; just before, he answered the Egyptians' claim by demanding wages for the years of slavery in Egypt.

people.name: Geviha ben Pesisa
people.about: Argues for the Jewish people before Alexander, with the Sages' permission.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: The ruler before whom the case is brought.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Sage who explains what Abraham's gifts to the concubines' sons were.

terms.meaning: A wife of Abraham; her sons were among those he sent away with gifts.
A deed by which a father divides his property among his sons during his lifetime.

note: Rabbi Yoḥanan taught that God will one day set gems thirty cubits square, with openings bored through them, as the gates of Jerusalem. A student mocked him: we cannot even find a gem the size of a dove's egg. Later, at sea, the student saw ministering angels cutting such stones, and they told him they were for the gates of Jerusalem. Back home he told Rabbi Yoḥanan: teach, master, it is fitting for you to teach; I saw just what you said. Rabbi Yoḥanan answered: good-for-nothing, had you not seen it, you would not have believed? You mock the words of the Sages. He set his eyes on him and turned him into a pile of bones.
why: Rabbi Yirmeya asked whether an elder's praise of a Sage's teaching was disrespect. Rabbi Zeira says no, it was support; real disrespect is this student's, who agreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan only once he had seen it for himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage whose teaching about the gates of Jerusalem the student mocked.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Tells this story in answer to Rabbi Yirmeya's question.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm.

note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students came to visit. He said there was fierce wrath in the world. They wept; Rabbi Akiva laughed. As long as his teacher's wine, flax, oil and honey never spoiled, Akiva said, he feared Rabbi Eliezer had already received all his reward; now, seeing him suffer, he was glad. Asked whether he had neglected any of the Torah, Akiva quoted his teacher's own lesson: no one on earth is so righteous that he never sins. In a second account, four Sages visit. Three praise him as better for Israel than rain, the sun, or parents; Akiva says suffering is precious. Rabbi Eliezer asks to be propped up to hear, and Akiva proves it from King Manasseh, whom only suffering turned back to God.
why: Just before, a verse is read to say that even when God brings illness, He heals. These visits to the sick Rabbi Eliezer turn to the value of suffering, and the discussion then follows Manasseh's repentance.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who fell ill and was visited by his students and colleagues.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's student, who laughed at his illness and taught that suffering is precious.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Visitor who called Rabbi Eliezer better for Israel than the sun.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya

terms.meaning: Got his whole reward in this life, leaving none for the World-to-Come.
